text: Hi Mozilla dot A.I. team. I'm Avie, and this is my Otari feedback for the Developers Wilding hackathon. I'll cover what I built, what worked well, what didn't, and what I would change.

First, what I built. Budget Buddy is an A.I. chat app for families and classrooms. Instead of everyone sharing one A.I. key and one surprise bill, each person gets their own weekly budget. A parent or teacher adds members, and each kid joins with a six letter code. On the left is the grown-up dashboard, with every member's cap, spend, and chats this week. On the right is a kid's chat, and under every answer you can see the real cost of that answer, and how much budget is left.

I used five Otari features. Chat completions through the OpenAI compatible endpoint, running an open weight model, Mistral Small 3. Request tags, so every call carries the member it belongs to. The inline cost, usage dot cost U.S.D., on every response. And on a self hosted Otari, virtual keys and users with weekly budgets. In that mode each member gets a real Otari key, and Otari itself refuses the request with budget exceeded once the week is spent.

Here is what one request looks like. A normal chat completion, with metadata naming the app, the member, and the group. The response comes back with its exact price in usage. Budget Buddy shows that number to the kid, and adds it to their week.

Second, what worked well. Otari was a true drop in. Any OpenAI style client works, I only changed the base U.R.L. and the key. Getting the exact cost on every response was my favourite part, because I never had to call a separate billing A.P.I. Budgets really stop spending, since Otari reserves the cost before it calls the model, and sends back a retry after time. Open weight models are cheap too. All my testing and demo takes cost about three hundredths of a cent. And because Otari is open source, I could read the code to understand how keys, users and budgets fit together.

Third, what didn't work. The big one: on hosted otari dot A.I., a normal tenant A.P.I. key can only chat. The keys, users, budgets and usage routes need the gateway's master key or a dashboard session. So on hosted, my app couldn't create a key and a budget for each family member, which was the core idea. The second problem was smaller. The dashboard shows a masked version of the key later on. I copied that one, and every call failed to authenticate until I made a fresh key. I added a start up check that warns when a masked key is pasted.

To get around the first limit, I built two modes. Managed mode, for a self hosted Otari, where each member gets a real key and budget, and Otari enforces the cap. And hosted mode, for otari dot A.I., where members share one key, every request is tagged, and my app adds up the cost and enforces each cap itself. The live demo runs in hosted mode.

Fourth, what's missing, and what I would change. Most of all, scoped admin keys on hosted. A tenant key that can create child keys, each with its own budget, would make apps like Budget Buddy work fully on hosted Otari. Next, a usage A.P.I. that works with a normal key, so apps can show spend per tag or per key. Budget alerts, like a webhook at eighty and one hundred percent. A clear copy it now warning when a key is created. And a family or classroom recipe in the docs.

To sum up the written questions. I was most tempted to skip Otari when hosted keys couldn't create per member keys and budgets. What I built myself was per member tagging and weekly caps from Otari's cost. And yes, I would keep using Otari for anything that needs spend limits, and even more once hosted keys can manage child keys.
Thank you for running this hackathon, and for building Otari in the open. The code and the live demo are linked here. Cheers!
